hook_text: Twelve knots. Three people. A perfect right angle, three thousand years ago.
clip_script:
Long before anyone wrote down a proof, surveyors in ancient Egypt needed right angles for the corners of fields and the bases of temples, and they had no set squares. What they had was a loop of rope with twelve equally spaced knots — twelve equal intervals around the loop.

Three people hold the rope. The first holds a knot. The second walks three intervals along and pulls tight. The third walks four intervals from the second and pulls tight, and the remaining five intervals run back to the first. The rope now forms a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 intervals, and the angle between the 3 and the 4 is a right angle, exactly, every time, in any field. Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five. A theorem made of hemp.
visual_style: A knotted rope loop pulled taut by three figures into a 3, 4, 5 triangle on sand; squares of 9, 16 and 25 dots bloom on its sides
pacing: slow pull, then the squares appear quickly
